title: A Quiet Cup of Tea
body: Mina visits her grandmother every Sunday for tea. Grandmother lives in a small house beside the park. The kitchen opens onto a bright room with a blue table. This Sunday, Grandmother plans to share tea with her old neighbor Lan. Lan lives across town now, but she still loves their tea talks. Mina hangs her coat on a hook and joins Grandmother in the kitchen. Grandmother takes a blue tin from the shelf and sets it on the table. "Lan likes plain tea," she says. "She takes no milk or sugar with her tea." Mina reads the label on the tin, though she knows the tea by its smell. They wash two cups and place them on a tray. Grandmother fills a kettle and puts it on the stove. Mina asks how many leaves fit in each tea cup. "A small spoon works well for one tea cup," Grandmother says. Mina takes the spoon and counts two small heaps of tea. A few leaves fall on the table. She laughs as tea leaves fall around the cup. Mina sweeps the dry leaves into a bin on the floor. As the kettle warms, they talk about Lan and the old tea stall. Grandmother met Lan at that stall by the school gate over tea. They sat at the stall after class and shared one cup of tea. After many years apart, Lan visits again for tea. Mina wonders if Lan remembers their long talks over tea. A clock on the wall says eleven. The water for tea is hot, so Grandmother lifts the kettle from the stove. She waits a short time before pouring, because a rolling boil can make green tea bitter. Mina watches tea fill each cup, one at a time. The pale tea smells fresh and light. Grandmother asks Mina to carry the tray into the front room. Mina holds the tray with both hands and walks slowly across the room. A soft knock sounds on the door. Lan stands at the door with an umbrella and a bag of tea. Her hair is wet, but the tea stays warm on the tray. Lan smiles when she sees Grandmother in the front room. They hug by the door, then sit at the table and pour tea. Lan puts her bag on the chair and opens it. Lan takes a small photo of the old tea stall from her bag and puts it on the table. "I found it in my desk last week," Lan says. Mina looks at the photo on the table. Two young women sit at a tea stall and laugh. Grandmother and Lan look just as happy in the picture. Mina pours tea for Lan, then takes a seat by the window. Lan lifts the cup and smells the tea before she drinks. "The tea has the same soft taste," she says. Grandmother asks what tea Lan makes in her new flat. Lan tells them about her garden and tea with a neighbor. Mina listens while she drinks her tea. The story makes the room feel bright, even as rain taps on the window. Lan asks Mina which books she reads, and Mina answers over tea. Mina tells her about a book while the tea cools on the table. Lan knows that story, too, and names the next book while rain taps on the window. Mina writes the title on a paper strip beside her tea cup. The women share tea and talk about small things for a long time. No one checks the clock on the wall. When the tea is gone, Grandmother offers another cup. Lan says yes to another cup of tea, and Mina prepares it. She measures the tea leaves, waits for the kettle, and pours slowly. The tea is not too strong this time. Lan says Mina makes a fine cup of tea. Mina feels proud of the tea, but she knows she can learn more. Before Lan leaves, they set a day for the next tea visit. Lan takes her bag but leaves the photo on the table for Mina. Mina puts the photo in her school bag beside the paper strip with the book title. The rain ends, and sun comes into the room. Lan waves from the gate as Mina stands in the doorway. Mina clears the cups and washes the tea pot. Grandmother says the visit and shared tea make the day special. Mina asks if she can make tea again next Sunday. Grandmother nods and saves the blue tin on the shelf. On Mina's walk across town, she thinks about Lan's stories and tea. She knows how to make the tea now, but she likes the talk best. After the visit, she tells her mother about Lan over one more cup of tea.
